books.title: Foundation Mathematics
books.subtitle: From counting to the doorstep of algebra
books.description: The ground floor of mathematics, built patiently from the act of counting: numbers and place value, the four operations and why they work, factors and primes, fractions, decimals and percents, ratio and proportion, elementary geometry and measurement, and the first taste of algebraic thinking. Every idea is introduced from zero, derived where a derivation exists, and drilled through graded exercises with full solutions — so that the books above it (Arithmetic & Number Systems, Elementary Algebra, Geometry…) can be climbed without gaps.

chapters.title: Numbers and Place Value
chapters.summary: Starts from the act of counting itself: what a number is, how numerals encode them with just ten digits, why place value makes the whole system powerful, and how the number line lets us see order at a glance. Closes with the two great naming conventions for large numbers — international and Indian.

lessons.title: Numbers, Digits and Place Value
lessons.unit: platform base (lesson 1.1 authored with the platform as pipeline validation)
concepts: International and Indian systems of numeration
objectives: Say precisely what a number, a numeral and a digit are — and never confuse them again
Break any whole number into its place values and write it in expanded form
Read and compare numbers in both the international and the Indian naming systems
Locate integers on the number line and use it to compare them

lessons.title: Comparing and Ordering Numbers
concepts: Digit count as the first comparison test
The domination bound: why the leftmost differing seat decides
Greatest and smallest numbers from given digits
Digit rearrangements preserve the digit sum
objectives: Compare any two whole numbers instantly and say which seat decided the answer
Arrange a mixed list of large numbers in ascending or descending order without pairwise struggle
Build the greatest and smallest possible numbers from a given set of digits
Explain, with a proof, why the leftmost differing digit always settles the comparison

lessons.title: Rounding and Estimating
concepts: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand
The midpoint convention: ties round up
When to round up on purpose (capacity problems)
objectives: Round any whole number to a named place and say which digit made the decision
Estimate sums, differences and products to a chosen level of coarseness — and choose the right level
Recognise when rounding a subtraction of close numbers destroys the answer, and what to do instead
State a guaranteed error bound for a sum of rounded numbers

chapters.title: The Four Operations
chapters.summary: Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — first as actions on quantities, then as algorithms on numerals, where the overflow argument from Chapter 1 returns as carrying and borrowing. Includes order of operations, estimation checks, and why division by zero is undefined.

lessons.title: Addition and the Art of Carrying
concepts: Why the carry is never more than 1
objectives: Explain addition as counting on, and show it as a jump on the number line
State and use the commutative, associative and identity properties of addition
Execute column addition with carries reliably — and prove why a carry can never exceed 1
Use the mod-9 digit-sum checksum to catch errors, and know exactly when it fails

lessons.title: Subtraction and Borrowing
concepts: Subtraction as the inverse of addition
Subtraction breaks closure, commutativity and associativity
Why one borrow is always enough
The inverse check and the nines complement
objectives: Explain subtraction as the missing-addend question — the inverse of addition — and read it as take-away or comparison
Show exactly which laws of addition die for subtraction, with a counterexample for each
Execute column subtraction with borrowing reliably, including the borrow-across-zeros ripple
Prove why a column ever needs to borrow exactly one — never two — and check any subtraction two independent ways

lessons.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition — and Beyond
concepts: Equal jumps on the number line
The laws that return: closure, commutative, associative, identity 1
Column multiplication as shifted partial products
objectives: Explain multiplication as repeated addition and as equal jumps on the number line — and why the two orders land in the same place
State the four laws multiplication shares with addition plus the new distributive law, and use each deliberately
Execute column multiplication as shifted partial products, knowing why the shift exists and how large its carries may grow
Bound a product's digit count before computing it, and check any product with the mod-9 fingerprint

lessons.title: Division, Remainders and Why Zero Never Divides
concepts: Sharing and grouping — the two readings
Equal jumps backwards: division as repeated subtraction
Division as the inverse of multiplication
The division algorithm a = q·b + r
Why division by zero is undefined
objectives: Read division both ways — equal sharing and grouping — and see each as undoing a multiplication
Execute long division as the multiply–subtract–bring-down loop, knowing why each step is lawful and where place value hides
Prove and use the remainder bound r < b, predict a quotient's digit count, and certify any division with the check a = q·b + r and the mod-9 fingerprint
Prove why division by zero has no answer — and why 0 ÷ 0 fails differently from 7 ÷ 0

lessons.title: Order of Operations and the Language of Expressions
concepts: Brackets: bar, parentheses, braces, square brackets
objectives: Read any string of numbers and operations as one expression with a single value — and distinguish expressions from equations
State the order-of-operations treaty: brackets first (bar, then ( ), { }, [ ]), then "of", then × and ÷ left to right, then + and − left to right
Justify why × outranks + by the compression argument, and say precisely which clauses of the treaty are forced and which are agreed
Simplify fully nested exam expressions with the bracket ladder, dodging the two great BODMAS traps
Gate every simplification with a rounding estimate before trusting it

chapters.title: Factors, Multiples and Primes
chapters.summary: The multiplicative structure of whole numbers: divisibility tests with reasons, prime factorisation, HCF and LCM by three routes, and a first meeting with the infinitude of primes.

lessons.title: Divisibility and Its Tests
concepts: Compound tests and the coprime split
objectives: Define divisibility through the division algorithm of Lesson 2.4 — d divides n exactly when the remainder is 0 — and use the d | n notation
Apply the tail tests for 2, 5, 10, 4, 25, 8 and 125, and derive them from the fact that 10^k = 2^k × 5^k
Prove the digit-sum tests for 9 and 3, apply the alternating-sum test for 11, and read actual remainders off both
Screen any number against every divisor from 2 to 12 in seconds, using the cheapest test first — and know why the parts in a compound test must be coprime

lessons.title: Prime Numbers and Factorisation
concepts: Why 1 and 0 sit outside the treaty
Trial division and the square-root licence
objectives: Define prime and composite numbers by counting factors, and explain why 1 (and 0) belong to neither family
Run the sieve of Eratosthenes up to 100 and recall the 25 primes it leaves behind
Certify primality by trial division, using the square-root licence to stop testing at √n — and spot the false primes 91, 87 and 221
Factorise any number completely into primes and state the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every road reaches the same atoms
Predict the number of divisors of any number from its prime exponents, via (a₁ + 1)(a₂ + 1)⋯(aₖ + 1)

lessons.title: Highest Common Factor
concepts: HCF as the greatest common divisor
Shared primes at the smaller powers
Bézout's identity and the crossroads lemma
objectives: Define common factors and the highest common factor, and read the HCF off two prime factorisations as the shared primes taken at the smaller powers
Run the Euclidean division method — the ladder of remainders — for two and three numbers, and justify it with the swap lemma
State Bézout's identity, prove it by back-substitution, and use it to discharge the crossroads-lemma debt that Lesson 3.2 left open
Generalise Lesson 3.1's coprime split into a theorem and deploy the three "greatest number" patterns that examinations recycle

lessons.title: Lowest Common Multiple
concepts: LCM as the first shared departure
Shared primes at the larger powers
objectives: Define common multiples and the lowest common multiple, and prove that the common multiples of a pair are exactly the multiples of their LCM
Compute the LCM by three routes — listing, prime factorisation at the larger powers, and the common-division ladder — and choose the right route for the job
Read the LCM off the Venn picture Lesson 3.3 drew, as the product of all three territories, and recognise the coprime and divisibility extremes
Deploy the four "least number" exam patterns — exact division, same remainder, equal deficiencies, and counting multiples — with reasons

lessons.title: HCF, LCM and How They Relate
concepts: Feasibility: the HCF must divide the LCM
objectives: Prove the product rule gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b from the Venn territories and the atoms
Rebuild a missing member from HCF, LCM and the known member — with the guard that the HCF divides every member
Rebuild whole pairs with the coprime-split engine, and count how many pairs share one fingerprint
Test any fingerprint for feasibility with one division, and unite the chapter's exam patterns in a single table

chapters.title: Fractions
chapters.summary: Why we need numbers between the integers, what a fraction really is, equivalence, comparison, the four operations on fractions, and the number line made dense.

lessons.title: The Idea of a Fraction
concepts: Fractions name parts of a whole
objectives: Say precisely what a fraction is — both as equal parts of a whole and as an exact division — and name its parts (numerator, denominator, vinculum)
Place any fraction on the number line between the right whole numbers, and convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers using the division algorithm of Lesson 2.4
Compute a fraction of a quantity, and read "how many 1/d-pieces fit in m" as the grouping division of Lesson 2.4
Prove that between any two different fractions there always lies another — the density that Lesson 3.5 promised — using the mediant

lessons.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplification
objectives: Recognise and generate equivalent fractions with the multiplying rule n/d = nk/dk, and explain it by regrouping equal pieces
Simplify any fraction to its lowest terms in one step via the HCF of chapter 3, and say why that name is the canonical one
Prove the cross-multiplication test a/b = c/d ⟺ ad = bc — paying, in full, the licence Lesson 4.1 borrowed for the mediant proof
Raise a fraction to any target denominator that is a multiple of its own — the move that powers common denominators in Lessons 4.3–4.4

lessons.title: Comparing Fractions
concepts: Unit fractions shrink as denominators grow
objectives: Decide which of two fractions with the same denominator or the same numerator is larger, and justify the verdict in terms of piece size and count
Compare any two positive fractions with the cross-multiplication test — two multiplications — and say why the products decide, on the common bd-ruler
Raise any set of fractions to one common ruler (the product of denominators or the LCM) and arrange them in ascending or descending order
Use the anchors 0, 1/2 and 1, the completing-the-whole view, and the wholes-first rule to compare mixed numbers and exam-style lists quickly

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts: Unlike fractions and the LCM method
Sums and differences in lowest terms
objectives: Add and subtract fractions on a shared ruler by counting pieces, and simplify every result to lowest terms
Raise any two unlike fractions to one common ruler — the LCM as standard equipment — and add or subtract the raised counts, with mixed numbers handled storey by storey
Read subtraction as gap-naming and complements, and decide when a subtraction has an answer at all
Split fractions into two-term sums of distinct unit fractions by the greedy choice, and prove why adding straight across never works

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
objectives: Multiply fractions straight across and simplify, read 'of' chains left to right, and cancel atoms before multiplying to keep every count small
Predict what multiplication does to size — proper multipliers shrink, improper ones grow, 1 holds — and verify the commutative, associative, identity and zero laws on fractions
Divide by any fraction through the reciprocal theorem, with the bd-ruler measurement count as the proof and the sharing reading as the small-divisor check
Compute the HCF and LCM of fractions with the banked shortcuts, push mixed numbers through the improper conversion, and settle exam word problems of the bottle, tank and ribbon families

chapters.title: Decimals and Percents
chapters.summary: Place value extended to the right of the point, the natural marriage of decimals and fractions, percent as a standardised fraction of 100, and the practical arithmetic of increase, decrease, discount and interest.

lessons.title: Decimal Places and the Point
concepts: The decimal point as a landmark
The atom test for exact decimal dress
objectives: Explain what the decimal point marks, read any decimal aloud correctly, and write decimals in expanded form across the extended place-value chart
Convert both ways across the fraction–decimal bridge: 10-family denominators directly, and any denominator built from 2s and 5s by re-cutting with the multiplying rule of Lesson 4.2
Prove and apply the atom test — a lowest-terms fraction wears an exact decimal dress if and only if its denominator carries no atoms but 2s and 5s, and the dress needs max(m, n) places
Locate decimals on the number line by zooming, compare and order them by aligning the points, and convert money, length and mass without the zero-filling traps

lessons.title: Decimals and Fractions, Two Ways of Writing the Same Numbers
concepts: Long division as the decimal machine
objectives: Run the long-division step machine past the point — multiply the remainder by ten, divide, record the digit — and justify why each step is legal
Classify any fraction in advance: terminating in max(m, n) places (only 2s and 5s), pure recurring (no 2s or 5s), or mixed recurring (a head of max(m, n) places, then a cycle)
Prove the dresses theorem by the pigeonhole argument on remainders, and read cycle lengths as the order of 10 modulo the denominator
Convert every recurring decimal back to its fraction by shift-and-subtract, and compare recurring decimals with truncated ones without being fooled

lessons.title: Operating on Decimals
concepts: The whole-number engine and the places-add rule
objectives: Add and subtract any decimals by aligning the points, padding with the trailing-zero licence and borrowing across the point, and check every subtraction by the inverse test
Multiply decimals with the whole-number engine and land the point by the places-add rule, proving the rule from the fraction reading, and shift the point by powers of ten without reordering a digit

Divide by whole numbers with the quotient's point riding the dividend's, and divide by decimals by clearing the divisor — scaling both numbers by the same power of ten and leaving the quotient untouched
Settle money, length and mass problems by converting first and operating second, and reduce every rate problem to one unit with the unitary method

lessons.title: Percent and Its Meaning
concepts: x% of y = y% of x
objectives: Read any percent as a fraction with denominator 100 and reduce it to lowest terms, including percents beyond 100 and decimal percents such as 12.5% and 6.25%
Convert both ways along the fraction–decimal–percent map with the two-hop law (÷ 100 one way, × 100 the other), and know where 33 1/3% is exact while 33.3% is not
Find x% of a quantity by the direct fraction-of and by the benchmark builds, and lighten the arithmetic with the commutativity gem x% of y = y% of x
Answer "what percent" and "find the whole" questions — the unitary method returning as the percent ladder — and read marks, shares and savings problems correctly

lessons.title: Percentage Change, Discounts and Simple Interest
objectives: Compute percentage increases and decreases as a percent of the original value, and carry them out as one multiplication by the factor (100 ± r)/100
Undo a percent change correctly — divide by the factor, never subtract the percent — and recover an original value from the changed one by the unitary method

Read the trader’s ledger: profit and loss percent reckoned on the cost price, discounts reckoned on the marked price, and the net effect of a markup followed by a discount computed by multiplying the factors
Price borrowed money with simple interest I = PRT/100 from the one-percent-a-year unit, form the amount A = P + I, and recover any missing letter of the formula

chapters.title: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
chapters.summary: Comparing quantities by division rather than difference: ratios in simplest form, unit rates, the cross-multiplication test for proportion, direct and inverse variation, and scaling in maps, recipes and models.

lessons.title: Ratio as a Comparison
objectives: Write and interpret ratios as part–part comparisons, and distinguish the ratio $a : b$ from the fraction $a/b$
Reduce any ratio — whole numbers, decimals or fractions — to its unique simplest form with the HCF, converting units first when they disagree
Generate and test equivalent ratios with the cross-test, and chain two pair-ratios into one continued ratio
Share a quantity in a given ratio with the one-part engine, and recover totals or individual shares from partial information

lessons.title: Rates and Unit Rates
objectives: Recognise a rate as a division comparison of quantities of different kinds, keep its units attached, and read it in either direction
Compute the unit rate by dividing — or by scaling to a friendly unit — and run it backwards to recover totals and counts
Compare offers, workers and journeys on one unit ground and in one direction, and expose the bulk and direction frauds
Use the speed family and the $\tfrac{5}{18}$ law between km/h and m/s, and average a journey honestly over its whole time

lessons.title: Proportion and Cross-Multiplication
objectives: State the definition of proportion, write it in the :: notation, and distinguish the statement $a : b :: c : d$ from the two ratios that build it
Prove and apply the cross law — the product of the extremes equals the product of the means — to test any claimed proportion with one multiplication per side
Fill a missing term in any seat of a proportion and solve rate-and-cost problems by proportion, checking against the unit-rate engine
Recognise continued proportion, find the mean and third proportional, and verify claims with $b^2 = ac$

lessons.title: Direct and Inverse Variation
objectives: State the definition of direct variation ($y/x = k$) and inverse variation ($xy = k$), and write both in the proportionality notation $\propto$
Certify which lock binds a table or a story — the constant-ratio test against the constant-product test — and refuse the grows-together fraud
Extend a certified direct rate and solve fixed-total problems by the constant product, the factor method and the flip, checking every answer against the fixed thing
Connect the chapter: the unit rate as $k$, the cross law inside the flip, and the line and hyperbola as the two graphs of the two locks

lessons.title: Scaling: Maps, Models and Recipes
objectives: State a map scale in all three dresses — verbal pair, representative fraction and bar scale — and convert between them across the km–m–cm bridge
Run the scale engine both ways — ground from map and map from ground — for maps, models and plans, and apply the area law: areas carry $m^2$, never $m$
Classify any scale drawing as reduction, life size or enlargement by its scale factor $m$, and see the factor laws of Lesson 6.4 at work in both directions
Scale a recipe up or down by the proved multiplier $q_2 = q_1 \times s_2/s_1$, keep every per-serving constant — and keep the clock off the ingredient list

chapters.title: Integers
chapters.summary: Negative numbers earn their place on the number line: temperatures, debts and directions; the sign rules derived rather than memorised; absolute value as distance, every counted gap recomputed as one subtraction in bars.

lessons.title: Negative Numbers and Why They Exist
concepts: Opposite quantities and the chosen zero
The integers and the symbol ℤ
The number line grows a left half
Absolute value as distance from zero
objectives: Say precisely why a system of counting numbers freezes the moment a quantity changes direction
Read any signed number by naming its chosen zero and its two directions
Locate, compare and order integers on the extended number line — including the −8 versus −3 trap
Find the opposite of any integer, and read the two hats the − sign wears
Evaluate first-look absolute values as distances from zero

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Integers
concepts: Addition as a walk on the line
The sign rules derived from the walk
objectives: Compute any sum of integers by walking the line, and state the two sign rules as derived shortcuts
Verify closure, commutativity, associativity, the identity and the inverse law for integer addition with instances
Rewrite any subtraction as adding the opposite and simplify every double-sign chain
Solve net-change word problems — balances, temperatures, dives — as chains of moves
Derive the zero-subtraction rules Brahmagupta stated in 628 CE from the movement model

lessons.title: Multiplying Integers and the Sign Rules
concepts: The sign rules derived, not decreed
The distributive law as the engine
A debt times a debt is a fortune
Sign parity for chains of factors
The multiplicative identity and the mirror-maker
objectives: Multiply any two integers by the two-step rule — magnitudes multiply, the sign table aims — and justify all four cases from the repeated-walk model
Reproduce both derivations of minus-times-minus: the forced staircase and the distributive argument
Verify closure, commutativity, associativity, the identity, the zero product property and the distributive law for integer multiplication with instances
Evaluate chains of factors by sign parity — an even count of minus signs lands positive, an odd count negative
Narrate products as signed quantities — falls per hour, waived penalties — and recover missing factors by the times table plus the sign rules

lessons.title: Absolute Value as Distance
concepts: Absolute value as distance from zero
objectives: Define absolute value as distance from zero, evaluate it by the piecewise rule, and justify why the rule never returns a negative
Verify the properties — non-negativity, the mirror property, the duality, the multiplicative property, the triangle fact — with instances and counterexamples
Order integers by magnitude and separate "greater number" from "greater size"
Compute the distance between any two integers as |a − b| = |b − a|, and re-read the chapter’s counted gaps — the lift, the Everest–Dead Sea gap, the Vostok–Phalodi gap — as one subtraction in bars
Solve absolute-value equations |x| = k — two answers for k > 0, one for k = 0, none for k < 0 — and explain each verdict geometrically

chapters.title: Geometry Foundations
chapters.summary: The visual half of mathematics begins and pays: points, lines, planes and angles as ideal objects; measuring angles; parallel lines and transversals; triangles and the angle-sum result; and the walk (perimeter) and fill (area) of the rectangle, the triangle and the circle — every formula derived from the tools before it.

lessons.title: Points, Lines and Planes
concepts: The ray — one endpoint, one direction
The plane as the flat stage
objectives: Define the ideal objects — point, line, ray, line segment, plane — and explain why every drawing is only a picture of them
Name segments, rays and lines correctly, and tell apart segment AB = segment BA from ray AB ≠ ray BA
State and use the two-point rule: exactly one line passes through two distinct points — and conclude that two distinct lines share at most one common point
Classify pairs of lines in a plane as intersecting or parallel, recognise concurrent triples, and count segments and lines among n points with N = n(n−1)/2
Re-read the number line as geometry: coordinates as points and 7.4’s distance formula |a − b| as the length of the joining segment

lessons.title: Angles and Their Measurement
concepts: The angle — two rays, one vertex
The degree and the 360° full turn
The protractor and the two-scale trap
The clock as an angle machine
objectives: Define the angle as two rays with a common endpoint, name its vertex and arms, and write it correctly in the vertex-middle convention
State the degree ledger — full turn 360°, half turn 180°, quarter turn 90° — and tell the honest story of why the circle carries 360 degrees
Classify any angle by size into the five names, including reflex measures recovered as 360° minus the protractor read
Measure angles with the protractor, defeat the two-scale trap with the sense check, and turn the clock face into an angle machine
Compute complements and supplements, prove the identity supp(x) − comp(x) = 90°, and count the angles determined by n rays with n(n−1)/2

lessons.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
objectives: Define a transversal, name all eight angles it creates at two crossings, and sort them into the interior band and the two exteriors
Prove the linear-pair law and the vertically-opposite theorem from 8.2’s straight-angle ledger — the two facts that hold at every crossing, parallel lines or not
State the corresponding-angles axiom (the school dress of Euclid’s fifth postulate) and derive the alternate-interior and co-interior consequences from it
Run the three parallel tests in both directions — to read every angle of a scene from one number, and to certify from measurements alone that two lines are parallel
Count the scene’s 28 angle pairs into the named families and recognise the F, Z and C memory patterns in any examination figure

lessons.title: Triangles and the Angle Sum
objectives: Define the triangle — three non-collinear points, three joining segments, and the region they enclose — and name its parts in both the capital-letter and the small-letter dress

Prove the angle sum property from the parallel through one vertex, spending exactly three tools already owned: the straight angle of 8.2, the alternate-interior theorem of 8.3, and the uniqueness of the parallel through a point
Derive the exterior angle property (exterior = the sum of the two remote interior angles) and its inequality reading, and use both to run exterior-angle chases
Classify triangles by sides (scalene, isosceles, equilateral) and by angles (acute, right, obtuse), and prove the one-right/one-obtuse law and the right-triangle complement reflex from the angle sum
Decide from three lengths alone whether a triangle exists, using the triangle inequality in its three-dress and largest-side forms

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area of Rectangles, Triangles and Circles
objectives: Define perimeter and area honestly — the walk around a figure and the fill inside it — and keep the two questions (and their units) apart for life
Derive the rectangle laws P = 2(l + b) and A = l × b from the walk and the tiling, and prove that a fixed perimeter never fixes an area (the square sweeps the board)
Derive the triangle formula A = ½ × base × height from the rectangle — two copies tile the box, and the altitude split cancels — and choose base-height dresses safely
Define π as the constant ratio C/d, derive C = 2πr and A = πr² (the sector rearrangement), and compute with both working values 22/7 and 3.14 at known accuracy
Convert area units by rescaling the tile (1 m² = 10⁴ cm², 1 hectare = 10⁴ m²) and dissect composite figures into the three measured shapes

chapters.title: Measurement
chapters.summary: What it means to measure: units as agreements, the metric system from first principles, unit conversion as multiplication by one, and the difference between precision and accuracy.

lessons.title: Units as Agreements
concepts: Measurement as a count of units
Quantity, unit, number — the three roles
The standard unit as an agreement
The inverse law — smaller unit, bigger count
objectives: Say exactly what a measurement is: a count of how many times a chosen unit fills the quantity — and read every measurement as number × unit
Explain why body units (handspan, cubit, pace) fail — the unit varies with the measurer — and name the three properties a good unit must have
State and prove the swap law n₁ × u₁ = n₂ × u₂, use it to move a quantity between units, and derive the inverse law: the unit shrinks k times, the count grows k times
Sort quantities into base (length, mass, time) and derived (area, speed, volume…), and read derived units as little formulas (m², m/s)
Tell the story of the worldwide agreement — from the cubit rods to the Metre Convention of 1875 to the SI of 1960 — and India’s own 1956/1960/2009 timeline

lessons.title: The Metric System
concepts: The metric system — one decimal family
Prefixes: kilo, hecto, deca, deci, centi, milli
The three school families: metre, gram, litre
The kilogram — the prefix-wearing base unit
The litre and the cubic decimetre
The 1795 law and the road to SI
objectives: Say what makes the metric system a system: every step between a unit and its multiples is the same step — a power of ten — and read the six school prefixes (kilo, hecto, deca, deci, centi, milli) with their factors
State and prove the point-shift law: h hops down the ladder multiply the count by 10^h, so converting is moving the decimal point, not doing arithmetic
Work the three school families — kilometre–metre–centimetre–millimetre, kilogram–gram–milligram, litre–millilitre — in both directions, including decimal quantities
Use the litre bridge (1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 L) to carry volume problems, and place the tonne on the mass rail

Tell the metre’s three bodies honestly — the Earth-quadrant definition of 1791, the platinum bar of 1799 (0.02% short, one part in 5,000), the light-speed metre of 1983 — and date the 1795 prefix law and the world’s adoption

lessons.title: Converting Units Without Memorising Tables
concepts: Multiplying by one changes the dress, never the quantity
The chain method — several hops in one line
The identity economy — six facts, every conversion
objectives: Build a conversion factor from any identity — a ratio of two equal measures, equal to 1 — and choose the dressing whose units cancel into the unit you want
Justify the method from 9.1’s $Q = n \times u$: multiplying by 1 preserves the quantity, and units cancel like factors
Run multi-hop chains in one line (km → m → cm; hours → minutes → seconds) and convert composite units such as km/h to m/s, re-deriving the 5/18 law of 6.2 instead of recalling it
Apply the squared-factor law honestly: $1\text{ m}^2 = 10^4\text{ cm}^2$ and $1\text{ m}^3 = 10^6\text{ cm}^3$ — the factor inherits the unit’s power — and refuse the classic ×100 area fraud
Run the direction test on every answer (smaller unit, bigger count) and diagnose upside-down factors from the shape of the units alone

lessons.title: Precision, Accuracy and Rounding in Measurement
concepts: Every measurement is a claim, not a fact
Precision — the fineness of the unit
Accuracy — closeness to the true value
Precision and accuracy are independent axes
Rounding to a named place — the digit rule
Significant figures — counting the honest digits
objectives: Explain why no measurement is exact — a reading names the unit-multiple nearest the truth — and read "7 cm" and "7.0 cm" as different claims about the same pencil
State the precision of a measurement as the smallest unit it distinguishes, and derive the interval law: a reading $m$ to the nearest unit $u$ confines the true value to $m - u/2 \le t < m + u/2$
Distinguish accuracy (closeness to the true value) from precision (fineness and repeatability), and diagnose a precise-but-inaccurate instrument from its pattern of readings
Round any number to a named place by the digit rule — including the half-up convention and the round-once-from-the-original discipline that defeats double rounding
Compute the greatest possible error of an instrument (half its smallest division) and count the significant figures a written measurement honestly carries

chapters.title: Data and Graphs
chapters.summary: Reading the world in tables and pictures: frequency tables, bar charts, line graphs, pie charts and when each lies or tells the truth; the mean, median and mode introduced honestly with their strengths and traps.

lessons.title: Collecting and Tallying Data
concepts: The raw list and why it defeats counting
The tally pass — one stroke per answer
Relative frequency — the table in percents
objectives: Say exactly what data is — the collected answers to a question, each one a value of the quantity asked about — and explain why a raw list defeats counting by re-reading
Run the tally pass honestly: one stroke per answer into its category’s row, the fifth stroke closing the gate, the frequency read as gates × 5 + leftovers
Build a frequency table from raw data and prove the check-sum law: because the categories partition the answers, the frequency column must sum to N — the table checks itself
Choose categories that do not overlap and leave no orphan answers — decided before collecting, with an "other" row as honesty’s catch-all
Convert a frequency table into relative frequencies (fractions and percents summing to exactly 1) and read comparisons straight off the rows

lessons.title: Bar Charts, Line Graphs and Pie Charts
concepts: The bar chart — the tally standing up
The scale — the y-axis is a ruler
The line graph — data with order (time)
The pie chart — parts of one whole
objectives: Draw and read a bar chart from a frequency table: equal-width bars in equal steps, the y-axis ruled as honestly as a ruler, the height × the scale reading rule
Prove the bar-scale law — a bar’s height in axis-steps IS the frequency, so doubling the answers doubles the bar — and choose an honest scale (equal steps covering the data)
Draw and read a line graph for ordered data (a time series): plot the points, join consecutive points, read each segment’s steepness as the change per interval
State the interpolation caution: the segments between measured points are guesses, not measurements — and refuse line graphs for unordered categories
Prove the central-angle law θ = (f/N) × 360° from the partition of 10.1, compute every slice angle from a frequency table, and name which graph fits which data shape

lessons.title: Reading Graphs Critically
concepts: A graph is an argument — check it
The truncated baseline — the classic lie
The mismatch gallery — wrong graph, wrong claim
objectives: Diagnose the truncated-baseline lie: a bar chart whose axis starts above zero breaks the bar-scale law, and quantify the damage with the exaggeration law
Prove and use the exaggeration law E = v₁(v₂−b)/(v₂(v₁−b)) — exactly 1 at a zero baseline, climbing without bound as the baseline creeps toward the data
Explain the twin-scales trap: rescaling a chart preserves within-chart comparisons (the bar ranking, the steepness order) but destroys cross-chart pixel comparisons
Refuse the mismatched graph — lines through unordered categories, pies that do not close on 360°, perspective-distorted 3D pies — and repair each with the honest alternative
Apply the five-question checklist (labelled axes? zero baseline? even steps? source? honest title?) and state the correlation-is-not-causation caution with a concrete third-variable example

lessons.title: Mean, Median and Mode
concepts: The mean — the total shared equally
The balance law — the deviations cancel
The rebuild law — total = N × mean
The median — the middle of the ordered list
The outlier and the honest average
objectives: Define and compute the arithmetic mean as the equal share of the pooled total, prove the balance law (the deviations at the mean sum to zero) and its rebuild corollary total = N × mean, and use both on frequency-table, missing-value and combined-mean questions
Locate the median of any ordered list — the value at position (N+1)/2 for odd N, the mean of the pair at positions N/2 and N/2 + 1 for even N — and prove the position law from the equal-sides demand
Name the mode of a frequency table in its three honest moods — unique, absent, and doubled — and explain why it is the only average a table of categories can support

Diagnose the outlier problem: quantify how one extreme value drags the mean (a change of Δ moves it by Δ/N) while the median and the mode refuse to move, and choose the honest average for the question asked
Read the three averages off one dataset and explain why they may disagree — the disagreement (27, 25.5 and 24 for one week of temperatures) is information, not error

chapters.title: Patterns and the Doorstep of Algebra
chapters.summary: Number patterns, sequences built by rules, matchstick and tile patterns expressed as formulas, and the first use of a letter for an unknown — the exact point where Elementary Algebra takes over the climb.

lessons.title: Patterns and Rules
concepts: The sequence: numbers with an order
Term-to-term rules and the two tests
The jump law — term n is n−1 jumps away
The famous families: evens, odds, squares
The triangular numbers and the handshakes
The gnomon law: the odds build the squares
objectives: Say exactly what a sequence is — numbers in a fixed order, each one a term, named $T_1, T_2, \ldots$ — and state the rule that generates a pattern in words before trusting any continuation
Apply the two term-to-term tests: constant differences certify an add-rule, constant quotients certify a multiply-rule — and explain why a test certifies only what the rule states
Prove and use the jump law $T_n = T_1 + (n-1)d$ — reach any term without walking the whole list — and cash it on the evens ($2n$), the odds ($2n-1$) and the matchstick counts ($3n+1$)

Build the famous families as patterns: the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10 (differences 2, 3, 4 — the handshakes at a party), the squares, and the Virahanka numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 (each term the sum of the two before it)
Derive and use the gnomon law $1 + 3 + \cdots + (2n-1) = n^2$ through the L-wrap picture, and explain why an unspoken rule — the circle game’s 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31 — is not a rule at all

lessons.title: From Patterns to Formulas
concepts: The an + b dress: Tn = dn + (T1 − d)
objectives: Write and use position-to-term formulas: dress any add-$d$ pattern as $T_n = dn + (T_1 - d)$, reading the difference and the first term straight off the dress
Derive the staircase formula $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$ by the pairing argument and cash it on the triangular numbers ($T_{100} = 5050$)
Derive the handshake formula $\frac{N(N-1)}{2}$ as the staircase formula’s corollary and compute meeting and tournament counts (30 friends → 435; 40 players → 780)
See a formula structurally: the matchstick row’s $3n + 1$ as the seed’s 4 sticks plus 3 for every square after — the fitted dress and the counted structure agreeing
Read formulas backwards by arithmetic undoing — which position holds 99? — while keeping equation solving itself for lesson 11.3

lessons.title: A Letter for the Unknown
concepts: Variable: the letter for an unknown
The undo machine: ax + b = c
objectives: Say exactly what an equation is — a sentence asserting that two expressions name the same number — and what solving means: finding every value of the variable that makes the sentence true, proven by substituting back
Derive the balance law from the meaning of equality (the same change to both sides keeps them equal, division by zero refused) and use its four moves: add, subtract, multiply, share
Solve one- and two-step equations of the shape $ax + b = c$ by the undo machine — undo the LAST operation first — and verify every solution ($3x + 1 = 31$ gives $x = 10$)
Turn word problems into equations and back: the ribbon split ($x + (x + 11) = 47$), the ages ($2b + 3 = 17$), the rectangle (6 by 12), the father-and-son collecting ($x + 4x = 50$)
Close the book on the doorstep it was named for: the letter now holds an unknown — Elementary Algebra takes over the climb from exactly here

books.title: Arithmetic and Number Systems
books.subtitle: Why arithmetic works — and how the number systems were built
books.description: The structural sequel to Foundation Mathematics. FM taught you to compute; this book proves why the computing rules hold. Positional naming in any base, the division algorithm, Euclid’s algorithm with its proof, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, congruences as an arithmetic of remainders, and the great extension ladder ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ — each rung built to repair a closure failure. Divisibility tests you have used since school are finally derived; √2 is finally proved irrational; the primes are finally shown endless. Cross-references Foundation Mathematics throughout; hands off to Elementary Algebra, Number Theory and Set Theory.

chapters.title: The Natural Numbers as a System
chapters.summary: Counting rebuilt from the successor idea: the number line as order, induction as the domino principle that proves statements about every natural number at once, and the least-number principle (well-ordering) as the engine behind every "take the smallest counterexample" argument — with the equivalence of the two principles proved and recursion defined.

lessons.title: The Architecture of Counting: Successors and Order
concepts: Injectivity: no two numbers share a successor
objectives: State the successor picture of counting and the axioms that govern it, and say what each axiom prevents
Say precisely what $a < b$ means in successor terms, and compare numbers by run length instead of vibes
Prove that order is transitive by concatenating runs
Prove that the chain 1, 2, 3, … never repeats a value and never ends

lessons.title: Induction: Proving for Every Number at Once
objectives: State the two conditions of induction and explain why together they cover every natural number
Prove the sum formulas — $\sum k$, the odd sums, the geometric sum — by induction, every algebraic move justified
Diagnose the two classic failures — a missing base and a missing step — through concrete instances
Prove the no-return lemma and close the order gaps Lesson 1.1 left open

lessons.title: The Least-Number Principle and Recursion
objectives: State the least-number principle precisely — including the nonempty clause — and use it to certify least-element searches
Prove that induction and the least-number principle are equivalent, in both directions
Run minimal-counterexample (descent) arguments, including the theorem that every $n \ge 2$ has a prime divisor
Define addition and multiplication by recursion, unroll values from the rules alone, and say why the arithmetic laws become theorems

chapters.title: The Division Algorithm and the Structure of Divisibility
chapters.summary: The theorem hiding under every long division: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b, existence proved by well-ordering and uniqueness by subtraction. Divisibility becomes algebra (the transitive and linear-combination laws), the Euclidean algorithm gets the proof FM omitted, Bézout’s identity is derived, and linear Diophantine equations ax + by = c are solved in full.
plannedLessons: The Euclidean Algorithm, Proven — and Bézout’s Identity
Linear Diophantine Equations

lessons.title: Division with Rest: The Division Algorithm
concepts: The division algorithm a = bq + r
Repeated subtraction as the proof in motion
objectives: State the division algorithm precisely and read $a = bq + r$ in both directions — building a dividend from a pair $(q, r)$ and pulling a pair out of a dividend
Prove existence by the descent argument, naming exactly where the least-number principle of Lesson 1.3 enters
Prove uniqueness from the remainder band, and show by instance why dropping the band kills it
Use $q$ and $r$ as data: rebuild dividends, find smallest and largest numbers with a given remainder, and certify any division with the check $qb + r = a$

lessons.title: The Algebra of Divisibility
objectives: Define $a \mid b$ through its multiplier certificate and translate freely between divides, measures, and remainder-zero
Prove and apply the laws of divisibility: transitivity, product compatibility, linear combinations, antisymmetry, and the order link
Exercise the cancellation form $ac \mid bc \Leftrightarrow a \mid b$ — and locate its limits with the $12 \mid 3 \cdot 4$ caution
Read the divisor lattice of a number off its factor chains, and use it as a picture of transitivity

chapters.title: Positional Systems and Other Bases
chapters.summary: Base ten unmasked as one instance of a universal machine: the representation theorem (every number has exactly one name in every base b ≥ 2, proved from the division algorithm), conversion in both directions, arithmetic genuinely inside other bases (addition and multiplication tables in base b), and the binary–hexadecimal world that runs every computer.
plannedLessons: The Representation Theorem: Every Number Has Exactly One Name
Converting Between Bases
Arithmetic in Other Bases
Binary, Hexadecimal and the Machine

chapters.title: Primes and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
chapters.summary: The atoms of multiplication: Euclid’s two-thousand-year-old proof that the primes never end, the sieve that hunts them, the fundamental theorem (unique factorisation) with both existence and uniqueness proved — uniqueness cashed through Bézout — and the counting consequences: divisor counts, the exponent of a prime in n!, and the trailing zeros of factorials.
plannedLessons: The Primes Never End: Euclid’s Proof and the Sieve
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
Divisors from DNA: Divisor Counts and Factorial Zeros
How the Primes Are Distributed

chapters.title: Congruences: The Arithmetic of Remainders
chapters.summary: Remainders promoted to numbers: congruence defined and its laws proved, the school divisibility tests finally derived (why casting out nines works, why 11 alternates signs), the unit digit of huge powers found through cycles, linear congruences solved, and a computationally verified glimpse of Fermat’s little theorem — the doorway to the Number Theory book.
plannedLessons: Remainders Become Numbers: Congruence Defined
Why the Divisibility Tests Work
The Unit Digit and Cycles of Powers
Linear Congruences and a Glimpse of Fermat

chapters.title: Building the Integers
chapters.summary: The first great extension, done honestly: the closure failures that force negative numbers (FM 7.1 felt them; here they are named), the actual construction of ℤ from ℕ as difference pairs with the equivalence relation proved, and the arithmetic laws of ℤ derived from the construction — the reader’s first ring, met as a building rather than a fact.
plannedLessons: The Closure Failures That Force Extension
Constructing the Integers from the Naturals
The Laws of Integer Arithmetic

chapters.title: Building the Rationals
chapters.summary: Fractions revealed as a constructed system: the equivalence of FM 4.2 re-founded as a relation on pairs, the field laws derived (every nonzero number finally gets a reciprocal), and the two structural theorems — the rationals are dense, and their decimal expansions terminate or repeat — proved from the division algorithm.
plannedLessons: From Fractions to the Rational System
The Field Laws: Division Joins the Family
Density and the Decimal Mirror, Proven

chapters.title: Irrationals and the Real Line
chapters.summary: The diagonal that broke the rationals: √2 proved irrational by the classical contradiction, the family of irrationals grown from the primes, the arithmetic behaviour of irrational + rational sorted into a proved table, and completeness met informally — the no-holes property that makes the real line the stage for all of analysis.
plannedLessons: The Diagonal of the Square: √2 Is Irrational
The Irrationals Are Everywhere
The Real Line: Order, Density and Completeness

chapters.title: Numeration Through History
chapters.summary: Five systems, one winner: tally and grouping, the additive symbols of Egypt and Rome (and why they resist arithmetic), the place-value systems that arrived too early — Babylonian base sixty and the Mayan base twenty with their missing-zero costs — and the Indian decimal revolution that made zero a number and carried the world’s arithmetic.
plannedLessons: Tallies, Groupings and Additive Systems
Place Value Before Its Time: Babylon and Mesoamerica
The Indian Decimal Revolution and Zero

chapters.title: The Map of Number Systems
chapters.summary: The synthesis: the great extension ladder ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ drawn as one story of repaired failures; congruence arithmetic at work guarding data (casting out nines as an error detector, the mod-11 checksum scheme); and the competitive-arithmetic toolkit — unit digits, factorial zeros, base conversions, remainder chains — unified as one congruence engine.
plannedLessons: The Great Extension Story
Numbers That Guard Data: Checksums and Casting Out Nines
The Toolkit Synthesis
